Clutch size in the Black swift (Cypseloides niger) is limited to a single egg, with females producing one clutch per year, a remarkably low fecundity compared to other apodids that often produce multiple broods. This annual reproductive output, yielding one egg per nest [N_R_i = one egg per nest], combined with the single yearly attempt [F_R_i = single yearly attempt], is consistent with the species' slow life-history strategy. Under the thermal conditions typical of an active, incubating adult operating at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the maximum daily reproduction rate is extremely low. This extreme iteroparity, characterized by an extraordinarily low annual fecundity, appears to be an adaptation to the unpredictable and ephemeral insect resources that Black swifts exploit during their high-altitude foraging forays over mountainous terrain. Field studies in the Pacific Northwest indicate that the single egg strategy may buffer against the high risks of nest failure common on cliff-face sites exposed to weather.

Neonatal mass in the Black swift, recorded from freshly laid eggs, begins at 5.11 grams [Ww0 = 5.11 grams] when measured as the initial wet weight of the newly fertilized ovum before any significant incubation. This is a relatively small egg mass for a swift of its body size, representing a substantial investment given that the altricial hatchling emerges at an even lower weight. At hatching, the chick weighs just 3.3 grams [Wwb = 3.3 grams], a remarkably diminutive size that underscores the extreme altricial state of the newborn. This low birth mass, less than a tenth of the eventual adult female weight, necessitates a prolonged period of intensive parental provisioning. Data gathered from nest monitoring in Colorado confirm that these light-bodied chicks require frequent feeds of compressed insect boluses to sustain their rapid growth during the initial weeks of life.

Under field conditions, where nest temperatures fluctuate more widely, the incubation period can vary by several days. The egg itself is incubated almost continuously, with parental shifts averaging several hours to ensure the embryo remains within the optimal thermal range for development. This synchronized effort allows the species to exploit brief windows of favorable insect abundance following hatching.
